mainEntity.name: What is type casting in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Type casting in Java is the process of converting a value from one data type to another. Java supports two kinds: (1) Primitive casting — converting between the 8 primitive types (int, double, char, etc.). (2) Object casting — converting between types in an inheritance hierarchy. Casting can be implicit (widening — done automatically by the compiler when no data loss is possible) or explicit (narrowing — done manually by the programmer using the cast operator (type) when data loss may occur).

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between widening and narrowing casting in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Widening casting (implicit): converts a smaller type to a larger type automatically — byte → short → int → long → float → double. No data loss occurs. No cast operator needed. Example: int i = 100; double d = i; // automatic. Narrowing casting (explicit): converts a larger type to a smaller type manually using the cast operator (type). Data loss (truncation) may occur. Example: double d = 9.99; int i = (int) d; // i = 9, decimal part lost. Widening is safe and automatic; narrowing is risky and must be done consciously.

mainEntity.name: What is upcasting and downcasting in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Upcasting: converting a subclass reference to a superclass reference. Always safe — done implicitly. Example: Dog d = new Dog(); Animal a = d; // upcasting — automatic. After upcasting, only the superclass methods are accessible via the reference. Downcasting: converting a superclass reference back to a subclass reference. Must be done explicitly with a cast operator. Can throw ClassCastException at runtime if the actual object is not of the target type. Always check with instanceof before downcasting: if (a instanceof Dog dog) { dog.bark(); } — pattern matching (Java 16+).

ClassCastException is a RuntimeException thrown when you attempt to downcast an object to a type it is not actually an instance of. Example: Animal a = new Cat(); Dog d = (Dog) a; // ClassCastException at runtime — a is a Cat, not a Dog. The compiler does not catch this because the cast syntax is valid — only the JVM can detect the mismatch at runtime. Prevention: always use instanceof to check the actual type before downcasting: if (a instanceof Dog dog) { dog.bark(); } — this eliminates ClassCastException entirely.

mainEntity.name: What is the instanceof operator and pattern matching in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: instanceof checks whether an object is an instance of a specific class or interface at runtime. Returns true or false. Example: Animal a = new Dog(); System.out.println(a instanceof Dog); // true. Pattern matching for instanceof (Java 16+): combines the type check and cast in one expression — if (a instanceof Dog dog) { dog.bark(); } — no separate cast needed. The variable dog is automatically bound and available in the if-block. Pattern matching eliminates the error-prone two-step (check then cast) pattern and is the modern, recommended approach for safe downcasting.

articleHeader.title: Java Type Casting — Widening, Narrowing, Upcasting, Downcasting & Best Practices
articleHeader.subtitle: Everything you need to know about Java Type Casting — what it is, widening (implicit) and narrowing (explicit) primitive casting, object casting (upcasting and downcasting), the instanceof operator, pattern matching, ClassCastException, and real-world production code examples.

sections.title: What is Type Casting in Java?

blocks.text: Type casting is the process of converting a value of one data type into another data type. Java is a statically typed language — every variable has a fixed type at compile time. However, there are many situations where you need to work with values across different types: storing an int result in a double variable, passing a subclass object where a superclass is expected, or retrieving an object from a collection and using its specific methods. Type casting is how Java handles all of these scenarios.

Java supports two categories of casting: Primitive casting — converting between the 8 primitive types (byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean). Object casting (Reference casting) — converting between types in an inheritance or interface hierarchy. Each category has two directions: widening (safe, automatic) and narrowing (risky, manual).

blocks.label: TypeCastingIntro.java
lines: // ── Primitive Widening — automatic, no cast operator needed ──────
long  longVal   = intVal;    // int → long — widening (implicit)
double doubleVal = intVal;   // int → double — widening (implicit)
// ── Primitive Narrowing — manual, cast operator required ──────────
int truncated = (int) price; // double → int — narrowing (explicit)
// ── Object Downcasting — manual, may throw ClassCastException ─────

blocks.title: 🔑 Type Casting at a Glance
blocks.text: Widening casting: smaller type → larger type. Automatic (implicit). No data loss. No cast operator. Example: int → double. Narrowing casting: larger type → smaller type. Manual (explicit). Possible data loss. Cast operator (type) required. Example: double → int. Upcasting: subclass → superclass. Automatic. Always safe. Example: Dog → Animal. Downcasting: superclass → subclass. Manual. May throw ClassCastException. Example: Animal → Dog. Rule of thumb: widening and upcasting are always safe; narrowing and downcasting require programmer responsibility.
Java type casting is classified into four types based on the direction of conversion and whether it involves primitives or objects.

items.title: Widening Casting (Implicit)
items.text: Converts a smaller primitive type to a larger one automatically. The compiler handles it without any instruction from the programmer. Order: byte → short → int → long → float → double. No data is lost. No cast operator is required. Example: int i = 100; double d = i; — automatic.

items.title: Narrowing Casting (Explicit)
items.text: Converts a larger primitive type to a smaller one manually using the cast operator (type). Data loss (truncation of decimal or higher bits) may occur. The programmer is responsible for ensuring the value fits. Example: double d = 9.78; int i = (int) d; — i = 9, decimal truncated.

items.title: Upcasting (Object Widening)
items.text: Converts a subclass object reference to a superclass (or interface) type. Always safe and done implicitly. After upcasting, only superclass members are accessible via the reference (subclass-specific methods are hidden). Polymorphism relies on upcasting — it is one of the most used patterns in Java.

items.title: Downcasting (Object Narrowing)
items.text: Converts a superclass reference back to its actual subclass type. Done explicitly with the cast operator. Can throw ClassCastException at runtime if the actual object is not of the target type. Always use instanceof before downcasting. Pattern matching instanceof (Java 16+) is the modern, safe way to downcast.

blocks.text: Widening casting happens automatically when you assign a value of a smaller type to a variable of a larger type. The Java compiler performs this conversion without any programmer instruction because there is no risk of data loss — the larger type can always hold the smaller type's full value range. The widening order for primitives is: byte → short → int → long → float → double. Note that boolean cannot be cast to any other type.

blocks.label: WideningCasting.java
lines: // ── Widening chain: byte → short → int → long → float → double ──
// ── Widening in expressions — automatic type promotion ─────────────
long  sum = x + y;   // int x is promoted to long automatically
double result = a / 2.0;  // a is promoted to double for this operation
// If a method expects double, passing int is valid — widening happens
int   charInt = ch;   // char → int: gives Unicode value

blocks.title: 📌 Widening Precision Note — int/long to float
blocks.text: Although widening from int or long to float is technically valid (float is larger in range), float has only 7 decimal digits of precision while int has up to 10 digits. This means very large int or long values may lose precision when widened to float. Example: int big = 123456789; float f = big; System.out.println(f); — prints 1.23456792E8 (not exactly 123456789). To avoid precision loss, widen to double (15 decimal digits) instead of float. This is a subtle, often-asked interview point: widening does not always guarantee complete accuracy for int/long → float.

Narrowing casting is the manual conversion from a larger data type to a smaller one using the cast operator: (targetType) value. Because the smaller type cannot always hold all values of the larger type, data loss is possible — decimal parts are truncated, and values outside the target type's range wrap around (overflow). The programmer must explicitly signal the intent to narrow using the cast syntax, making the potential loss of information intentional and visible in the code.

blocks.label: NarrowingCasting.java
lines: // ── double → int: decimal part is truncated (not rounded) ─────────
// ── long → int: higher bits may be lost if value > Integer.MAX_VALUE
int  trunced = (int) bigLong;     // Overflow — bits are chopped
// ── int → byte: wraps around if out of byte range (-128 to 127) ──
byte fitByte  = (byte) fitInt;   // 100 fits in byte range
// ── int → char: converts to Unicode character ────────────────────
// ❌ Common mistake: both are int — result is int, then widened
double wrong   = total / count;      // 3.0 (integer division first)

blocks.title: ⚠️ Narrowing Always Truncates — Never Rounds
blocks.text: When narrowing from double or float to int, Java always truncates toward zero — it does NOT round. (int) 9.9 = 9, not 10. (int) -9.9 = -9, not -10. If you need rounding, use Math.round() first: (int) Math.round(9.9) = 10. Also, if the value is outside the target type's range (e.g., casting 300 to byte whose range is -128 to 127), the result is not an error — the bits are silently truncated and the result wraps around. This produces unexpected values with no exception or warning. Always validate the value range before narrowing if overflow is a concern.
The table below summarizes all key differences between widening and narrowing casting side by side.

sections.title: char and Numeric Casting — Special Behavior

blocks.text: char in Java is a 16-bit unsigned integer representing a Unicode code point (0 to 65,535). It occupies a unique position in the casting hierarchy — it can be widened to int, long, float, or double, but converting between char and byte/short always requires an explicit cast in both directions. Understanding char arithmetic is a frequent interview and tricky question topic.

blocks.label: CharCasting.java
lines: // ── char → int: widening — gives Unicode (ASCII) value ────────────
char letter  = (char) code;  // int → char: gives character 'B'
// ── char arithmetic — result is int, not char ─────────────────────
System.out.println((char)(c + 1)); // B  — cast back to char
String str = "" + 'A' + 'B';  // "AB" — char appended as char
String str2 = 'A' + 'B' + "";  // 131"" — arithmetic first, then concat
char  c2 = (char) b;  // byte → char: explicit cast required
byte  b2  = (byte) c3; // char → byte: explicit cast required

blocks.title: ⚠️ char Arithmetic Produces int — Not char
blocks.text: When you perform arithmetic on char values, the result is int — not char. char c = 'A'; System.out.println(c + 1); prints 66, not 'B'. To get a char result from char arithmetic, you must cast back: (char)(c + 1) = 'B'. This is a very common tricky question in Java interviews: 'What is the output of System.out.println('A' + 1);' — answer is 66, not A1 or B. Also: 'A' + 'B' = 131 (int addition), but "" + 'A' + 'B' = "AB" (string concatenation). Order matters when mixing char and String with + operator.

Object casting (reference casting) involves converting object references within an inheritance hierarchy. Unlike primitive casting which converts the actual value, object casting only changes the type of the reference — the actual object in memory does not change. There are two directions: upcasting (subclass → superclass) and downcasting (superclass → subclass). Object casting is the foundation of Java polymorphism and is essential for writing flexible, extensible code.

blocks.label: AnimalHierarchy.java — Setup for examples
lines: // ── Hierarchy used in all object casting examples ────────────────────────
void speak() { System.out.println(name + " makes a sound."); }
void fetch() { System.out.println(name + " fetches the ball!"); }

blocks.text: Upcasting converts a subclass reference to a superclass (or interface) reference. It is always safe and done implicitly — no cast operator is needed. After upcasting, you access the object through the superclass reference, so only superclass members are visible at compile time. However, at runtime, overridden methods in the subclass are still called (dynamic dispatch / runtime polymorphism). Upcasting is the mechanism that enables polymorphism — storing different subclass objects in a superclass-typed variable or collection.

blocks.label: Upcasting.java
lines: // ── Implicit upcasting — no cast operator required ────────────────
Animal animal = dog;   // Upcasting: Dog reference → Animal reference
// The actual object in memory is still Dog — only the reference type changed
animal.eat();    // ✅ Works — eat() is in Animal
animal.speak();  // ✅ Works — calls Dog's speak() via dynamic dispatch!
// Output: Bruno says: Woof!  (NOT 'Bruno makes a sound.')
// animal.fetch(); // ❌ Compile error — fetch() not in Animal
// Even though the actual object is Dog, compiler sees Animal reference
Animal a1 = new Dog("Rex");   // Implicit upcasting
Animal a2 = new Cat("Whiskers"); // Implicit upcasting
a.speak();  // Calls correct subclass method at runtime
makeAnimalSpeak(new Dog("Buddy")); // Dog passed as Animal — upcasting
makeAnimalSpeak(new Cat("Kitty")); // Cat passed as Animal — upcasting
static void makeAnimalSpeak(Animal a) {  // Accepts any Animal subclass
a.speak();   // Correct subclass speak() called at runtime

blocks.title: 💡 Upcasting & Runtime Polymorphism
blocks.text: After upcasting, the compile-time type is the superclass (Animal) — so only superclass methods are accessible via the reference. But the runtime type is still the original subclass (Dog). When an overridden method is called, Java executes the subclass's version (dynamic dispatch). This is why a.speak() calls Dog's Woof! even though a is typed as Animal. This behaviour is the foundation of the Liskov Substitution Principle and polymorphic design: write code for the superclass/interface, supply any compatible subclass object.

Downcasting converts a superclass reference back to a subclass reference so you can access subclass-specific members. It must be done explicitly with the cast operator (SubclassType). Downcasting is only valid when the actual runtime object is of the target subclass type. If it is not, Java throws a ClassCastException at runtime. Always use instanceof to verify the type before downcasting.

blocks.label: Downcasting.java
lines: Dog dog = (Dog) animal;  // Explicit downcast — cast operator required
dog.fetch();             // ✅ Now subclass-specific method is accessible
Animal animal2 = new Cat("Luna");  // Actual object is Cat
// Dog dog2 = (Dog) animal2;        // ❌ ClassCastException at runtime!
// Compiler allows it (reference types are compatible)
// JVM throws at runtime: Cat cannot be cast to Dog
// ── Safe downcasting with instanceof (Java 14 and earlier) ─────────
if (b instanceof Dog d) {         // Check + cast + bind in one step
d.fetch();                    // ✅ d is already Dog — no separate cast
Animal[] animals = { new Dog("Bruno"), new Cat("Luna"), new Dog("Rex") };
// ── Downcasting null — always returns null, no exception ───────────
Dog    nullDog    = (Dog) nullAnimal;  // ✅ null cast is fine

blocks.text: The instanceof operator checks at runtime whether an object is an instance of a specific class or interface. It returns true or false. Before Java 16, the idiom for safe downcasting required two steps: check with instanceof, then cast. Java 16 introduced pattern matching for instanceof (JEP 394), which combines the check and cast into a single expression — eliminating boilerplate and the possibility of an incorrect cast.

blocks.label: InstanceofPatternMatching.java
lines: System.out.println(a instanceof Animal); // true  (Dog IS-A Animal)
System.out.println(a instanceof Dog);    // true  (actual type is Dog)
System.out.println(a instanceof Cat);    // false (not a Cat)
System.out.println(nullAnimal instanceof Animal); // false — null is never instanceof
// ── OLD WAY (pre-Java 16): check then cast — verbose ──────────────
Dog dog = (Dog) a2;    // Separate cast — redundant
// ── MODERN WAY (Java 16+): pattern matching — check + bind ─────────
if (a3 instanceof Dog dog) {  // If a3 is Dog, bind it to 'dog'
// ── Pattern matching in switch (Java 21 — fully standard) ──────────
case Dog dog -> dog.name + " is a dog who can fetch.";
case Cat cat -> cat.name + " is a cat who purrs.";
// Buddy is a dog who can fetch.

blocks.title: 💡 Always Use Pattern Matching instanceof for Downcasting
blocks.text: From Java 16 onwards, always prefer pattern matching instanceof over the old two-step check-then-cast pattern. Old: if (a instanceof Dog) { Dog d = (Dog) a; d.fetch(); } — two lines, redundant cast, error-prone if you forget the check. New: if (a instanceof Dog d) { d.fetch(); } — one line, no separate cast, eliminates ClassCastException. The bound variable (d) is only in scope inside the if-block where the check passed, so it is guaranteed to be of the correct type. In Java 21+, extend this to switch pattern matching for clean, exhaustive type dispatch without any instanceof verbosity.

sections.title: ClassCastException — What It Is and How to Prevent It

blocks.text: ClassCastException is a RuntimeException thrown by the JVM when you attempt to downcast an object to a type that is not compatible with its actual runtime type. The compiler cannot detect this because the syntax is valid — the mismatch only becomes apparent at runtime when the JVM checks the actual type. ClassCastException is entirely preventable by always checking with instanceof before downcasting.

blocks.label: ClassCastExceptionDemo.java
lines: Animal animal = new Cat("Luna");  // Actual type: Cat
// Dog dog = (Dog) animal;          // ❌ ClassCastException at runtime
// java.lang.ClassCastException: class Cat cannot be cast to class Dog
// ── Why does the compiler allow it? ───────────────────────────────
// Dog and Cat are both subclasses of Animal.
// The compiler sees: Animal reference → Dog reference.
// This cast is syntactically valid (they share a hierarchy).
// Only the JVM at runtime knows the actual object is Cat, not Dog.
System.out.println("Not a dog — skip fetch."); // This prints
// Cast failed: class Cat cannot be cast to class Dog
// Using try-catch for ClassCastException is an anti-pattern.
// Use instanceof to prevent it; don't catch it to handle it.

blocks.title: ⚠️ ClassCastException — Key Facts
blocks.text: ClassCastException is a RuntimeException — not caught at compile time. It is thrown only during downcasting — never during upcasting. The exception message tells you what the actual type was and what cast was attempted: class Cat cannot be cast to class Dog. Root cause: trying to use an object as a type it is not actually an instance of. Prevention: ALWAYS use instanceof before downcasting. Modern approach: use pattern matching instanceof (Java 16+) — it eliminates the need for a separate cast and makes ClassCastException impossible in that code path. Casting null never throws ClassCastException — null can be cast to any reference type and produces null.

Object casting works with interfaces as well as classes. A class that implements an interface can be upcast to the interface type, and an interface reference can be downcast to the concrete class type. Interface casting enables loose coupling — code depends on the interface contract, not the specific implementation. This is the basis of patterns like Dependency Injection, Strategy, and the Service Layer pattern.

blocks.label: InterfaceCasting.java
lines: class Duck extends Animal implements Flyable, Swimmable {
@Override public void fly()  { System.out.println(name + " is flying!"); }
@Override public void swim() { System.out.println(name + " is swimming!"); }
@Override public void speak(){ System.out.println(name + " says: Quack!"); }
public void waddle()          { System.out.println(name + " is waddling."); }
// flyer.swim();   // ❌ Compile error — Flyable doesn't have swim()
// flyer.waddle(); // ❌ Compile error — Flyable doesn't have waddle()
s.swim();   // ✅ Donald is swimming — Duck implements both
// ── Interface reference in a collection — polymorphism ─────────────
// Could add other Flyable implementations here
sw.swim();  // Only if the flyer can also swim

sections.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls — Casting Bugs That Fool Everyone

blocks.text: These are the most frequent casting-related mistakes in Java — from beginner oversights to experienced developer slip-ups under time pressure.

blocks.label: CastingMistakes.java
lines: // ❌ MISTAKE 1: Integer division before double assignment
double result = a / b;        // 3.0 — division done as int first!
// ❌ MISTAKE 2: Assuming narrowing rounds — it truncates
// ✅ Fix: use Math.round() if you need rounding
// Dog dog = (Dog) a2;        // ❌ ClassCastException at runtime
// ❌ MISTAKE 4: int → long overflow — forgetting L suffix
// long big = 10000000000;    // ❌ Compile error: int literal out of range
// ❌ MISTAKE 5: char + char gives int, not char
System.out.println("" + c1 + c2);      // AB  — string concat
// ❌ MISTAKE 6: Casting unrelated types — compile error
// String s = (String) new Integer(5); // ❌ Compile error — incompatible types
// Only types in the same hierarchy can be cast
// ❌ MISTAKE 7: int to byte overflow — silent wrap
byte small = (byte) big2;  // -56 — wraps silently, no exception
// ❌ MISTAKE 8: Casting long result of int multiplication
long product = x * y;       // ❌ -1474836480 — overflow! int*int first
// ✅ Fix: cast one operand to long before multiplication
// ❌ MISTAKE 9: Confusing compile-time type with runtime type after upcast
// anm.fetch();  // ❌ Compile error — Animal doesn't have fetch()
// Even though actual object is Dog, compiler only sees Animal reference
// ✅ Fix: downcast to access subclass methods

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These anti-patterns around type casting indicate design problems. Frequent casting is usually a signal that something in the class hierarchy or architecture can be improved.

items.title: Downcasting Without instanceof Check
items.text: Writing Dog d = (Dog) animal; without first verifying with instanceof is like reaching into a bag blindly. If the object is not a Dog, you get a ClassCastException at runtime. Always precede a downcast with instanceof — or better, use Java 16+ pattern matching: if (animal instanceof Dog d) { d.fetch(); }. A ClassCastException in production is entirely preventable — its presence in code indicates the developer skipped the safety check.

items.title: Catching ClassCastException as Flow Control
items.text: Using a try-catch around a downcast to handle the wrong type is an anti-pattern: try { Dog d = (Dog) a; } catch (ClassCastException e) { /* handle */ }. This is expensive (exceptions are costly), hides intent, and signals a design problem. The correct approach is instanceof. Exceptions are for exceptional situations — a type mismatch you can predict and check for is not exceptional, it is a design decision.

items.title: Excessive Downcasting in Business Logic
items.text: If your code frequently downcasts from a superclass to specific subclasses to call subclass methods, it is a sign of violated Liskov Substitution Principle or missing polymorphism. The fix is usually to move the specific behaviour into a method defined in the superclass/interface and overridden in each subclass — so the caller never needs to downcast. Downcasting should be rare in well-designed object-oriented code.

items.title: Using Object as a Universal Container
items.text: Storing everything as Object and casting back later — common in pre-Java-5 code — is an anti-pattern. Java generics (List<Dog> instead of List<Object>) eliminate the need for casting when working with collections. Every cast from Object requires a runtime type check and introduces risk. Use generics, sealed classes, or properly typed interfaces instead of raw Object references.

items.title: Narrowing Without Range Validation
items.text: Casting a long or int to byte, short, or char without verifying the value fits in the target type's range. Silent overflow produces completely wrong values with no error: (byte) 200 = -56. Before narrowing, always check: if (value >= Byte.MIN_VALUE && value <= Byte.MAX_VALUE) { byte b = (byte) value; }. Alternatively, use Math.toIntExact() or similar guard methods that throw ArithmeticException on overflow instead of silently wrapping.

items.title: Forgetting Cast Precedence in Expressions
items.text: Writing double result = (double)(a / b) instead of (double) a / b — the former casts the integer result of the division (3), giving 3.0. The latter promotes a to double before dividing, giving 3.5. Cast precedence is lower than most operators — the cast applies to the immediately following expression token, not the whole right-hand side. When in doubt, use parentheses explicitly: ((double) a) / b.

sections.title: Java Type Casting Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java developer interviews at all levels. Type casting, ClassCastException, instanceof, and widening/narrowing are high-frequency topics.

items.q: Q1. What is type casting in Java? How many types are there?
items.a: Type casting is converting a value from one data type to another. Java has two categories: (1) Primitive casting — converting between the 8 primitive types. Has two forms: widening (implicit, smaller to larger, automatic, safe) and narrowing (explicit, larger to smaller, requires cast operator, possible data loss). (2) Object casting — converting between reference types in an inheritance hierarchy. Also has two forms: upcasting (subclass to superclass, implicit, always safe) and downcasting (superclass to subclass, explicit, may throw ClassCastException). So in total: widening, narrowing, upcasting, downcasting — four types.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between widening and narrowing casting?
items.a: Widening: smaller primitive to larger (byte→short→int→long→float→double). Implicit — no cast operator. No data loss. Always safe. Example: int i = 100; double d = i; — d = 100.0. Narrowing: larger primitive to smaller. Explicit — cast operator required: (targetType). Data loss possible: decimal truncation or value overflow/wrap. Example: double d = 9.99; int i = (int) d; — i = 9 (decimal dropped). Key distinction: widening is automatic because it is always safe; narrowing requires programmer intent because it is potentially lossy.

items.q: Q3. What is the difference between upcasting and downcasting in Java?
items.a: Upcasting: converting a subclass reference to a superclass (or interface) reference. Implicit — no cast operator needed. Always safe — a Dog IS-A Animal, so storing a Dog reference in an Animal variable is always valid. After upcasting, only superclass members are accessible via the reference (subclass-specific members hidden). Downcasting: converting a superclass reference back to a subclass reference. Explicit — cast operator required. Can throw ClassCastException if the actual runtime type is not the target subclass. Always use instanceof before downcasting. Pattern matching instanceof (Java 16+) is the modern safe approach: if (animal instanceof Dog d) { d.fetch(); }.

items.q: Q4. What is ClassCastException? When does it occur?
items.a: ClassCastException is a RuntimeException thrown when you attempt to downcast an object to an incompatible type. Example: Animal a = new Cat(); Dog d = (Dog) a; — ClassCastException: Cat cannot be cast to Dog. The compiler allows the syntax because Dog and Cat are both in the Animal hierarchy — the incompatibility is only known at runtime when the JVM checks the actual object type. ClassCastException never occurs during upcasting. It never occurs when casting null. Prevention: always use instanceof before downcasting — or use pattern matching instanceof (Java 16+) which eliminates the ClassCastException risk in that code path entirely.

items.q: Q5. What is the output? int a = 7, b = 2; double result = a / b; System.out.println(result);
items.a: Output: 3.0. Reason: a and b are both int. Division of two ints in Java is integer division — the result is 3 (remainder discarded). The int result 3 is then widened to double, giving 3.0 — not 3.5. This is a very common beginner mistake. Fix: cast one operand before the division: double result = (double) a / b; — this gives 3.5. Note: double result = (double)(a / b); still gives 3.0 — integer division happens first, then 3 is cast to double. Cast must happen BEFORE the division.

items.q: Q6. What is the instanceof operator? What is pattern matching instanceof?
items.a: instanceof checks at runtime whether an object is an instance of a specific type. Returns true or false. instanceof null always returns false. Pre-Java 16 idiom (two steps): if (a instanceof Dog) { Dog d = (Dog) a; d.fetch(); }. Pattern matching instanceof (Java 16+, JEP 394): if (a instanceof Dog d) { d.fetch(); } — combines the type check and cast in one expression. If the check passes, the variable d is automatically bound to the cast result and available in the if-block. Pattern matching eliminates the redundant explicit cast, is more concise, and makes ClassCastException impossible in that code path. Java 21 extends this to switch expressions for exhaustive type-based dispatch.

items.q: Q7. What is the output of System.out.println('A' + 1)? What about System.out.println("" + 'A' + 1)?
items.a: Output 1: 66. 'A' has Unicode value 65. 'A' + 1 is char + int arithmetic — char is widened to int (65), then 65 + 1 = 66 (int). The result is an int, not a char. To get 'B', cast back: (char)('A' + 1). Output 2: A1. "" + 'A' evaluates left-to-right: empty String + 'A' = "A" (char appended as character in string context). Then "A" + 1 = "A1" (int 1 appended as string). This demonstrates operator left-to-right evaluation and the difference between arithmetic addition and string concatenation with +.

items.q: Q8. Can you cast a String to int in Java? How do you convert String to int?
items.a: No — you cannot cast a String to int. String and int are completely unrelated types — they are not in the same hierarchy and do not share any common type (except Object, but Object cannot be cast to int since int is primitive). Attempting String s = '42'; int i = (int) s; is a compile error. Correct conversion: use parsing methods — int i = Integer.parseInt('42'); or int i = Integer.valueOf('42'). These are not casts — they are conversions using library methods. Similarly: double d = Double.parseDouble('3.14'). If the string is not a valid number, parseInt throws NumberFormatException. This is a deliberate design: casting is for type-safe hierarchy conversions; parsing is for string-to-value transformation.

items.q: Q9. Does widening from int to float cause data loss?
items.a: Technically yes, in specific cases. Although float has a larger range than int, float only has 7 decimal digits of precision while int can represent integers up to 10 digits. For large int values (above ~16 million), widening to float may produce a slightly different value due to precision limits. Example: int big = 123456789; float f = big; System.out.println(f); — may print 1.23456792E8 (not exactly 123456789). This does not cause a compile error or warning — Java allows the widening even though precision is lost. To avoid this, widen to double (15-16 digits of precision) instead of float. This is an interview-level subtlety about the int→float widening.

items.q: Q10. What happens when you cast a value outside a type's range? Example: (byte) 130.
items.a: (byte) 130 = -126. byte range is -128 to 127. 130 does not fit in a byte. Java truncates to the lowest 8 bits of the binary representation of 130. 130 in binary: 10000010. As a signed 8-bit value (two's complement): the leading 1 means negative. Value = -(256 - 130) = -126. This is called overflow or bit truncation. No exception is thrown — Java silently produces the wrapped value. This behaviour applies to all narrowing casts where the value exceeds the target type's range. To detect and prevent this, check the range before narrowing: if (value >= Byte.MIN_VALUE && value <= Byte.MAX_VALUE) { byte b = (byte) value; } or use Math.toIntExact() for long→int which throws ArithmeticException on overflow.

Java widens a to double (5.0) for the comparison: 5.0 == 5.0 = true. This demonstrates automatic widening in assignment AND in comparison expressions. The compiler promotes the smaller type when comparing mixed types.

Output: 9, 9.99. (int) d: narrows double 9.99 to int by truncating the decimal — result is 9. The original variable d is unchanged — casting creates a new value, it does not modify d. This shows that narrowing is a conversion (produces a new value) not a mutation. d still holds 9.99. If rounding is needed: (int) Math.round(d) = 10.

Compiles but throws ClassCastException at runtime. The compiler allows the cast because Cat and Dog are in the same hierarchy (both extend Animal). At runtime, the JVM checks: is the actual object (Cat) an instance of Dog? No — so ClassCastException is thrown. Fix: if (a instanceof Dog dog) { dog.fetch(); } — this checks first and only casts if safe. With the instanceof check, the fetch() line is simply skipped because Luna is a Cat, not a Dog.

Output: -727379968, 1000000000000. x * y: both x and y are int. int * int = int. 1000000 × 1000000 = 1,000,000,000,000 which exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE (2,147,483,647) — overflow. The result wraps to -727379968 and is then widened to long. But the damage is done — the overflow happened before widening. (long) x * y: x is cast to long first: 1000000L. Then 1000000L * 1000000 — int y is widened to long for the operation. 1000000L × 1000000L = 1000000000000L — correct. Key rule: cast to long BEFORE multiplication when the result may overflow int.

Output: 131, AB, AB, 131. Line 1: 'A'(65) + 'B'(66) — char + char = int arithmetic = 131. Line 2: "" + 'A' = "A" (string concat, char as character), then "A" + 'B' = "AB". Left-to-right. Line 3: 'A' + "" = "A" (char + String = String concat), then "A" + 'B' = "AB". Line 4: 'A' + 'B' = 131 (both chars, arithmetic first — left to right), then 131 + "" = "131" (int + String = String concat). Rule: when + involves a String on EITHER side, it is concatenation. When both operands are numeric (int/char/etc), it is arithmetic. Evaluation is strictly left-to-right.

Output: -56, 56, 127, -128. byte range: -128 to 127. For out-of-range values, Java takes the value modulo 256, then interprets as signed byte. (byte) 200: 200 mod 256 = 200. As signed 8-bit: 200 - 256 = -56. (byte) -200: -200 mod 256 = 56 (positive, within byte range). As signed 8-bit: 56. (byte) 127: exactly at max byte value — 127. (byte) 128: 128 - 256 = -128 — exactly at min byte value. No exception thrown for any of these — silent wrap. This demonstrates the importance of range validation before narrowing casts.

Two issues — one style, one design. Style issue: the old two-step instanceof-then-cast pattern. Fix with pattern matching: if (a instanceof Dog d) { d.fetch(); } else if (a instanceof Cat cat) { cat.purr(); } else if (a instanceof Bird bird) { bird.sing(); }. Design issue (more important): frequent downcasting signals a violation of the Open-Closed Principle. Every new Animal subclass requires adding a new else-if here. Better design: add the specific behaviour as an abstract method in Animal — abstract void makeSound(); — and override it in each subclass. Then: a.makeSound(); — no casting, no if-else chain, works automatically for any current or future subclass. Use downcasting only when you genuinely need subclass-specific behaviour that cannot be expressed in the superclass contract.

sections.title: Conclusion — Type Casting: Converting Types Safely and Intentionally

blocks.text: Type casting is an essential Java skill that connects the type system to real-world programming needs. Mastering the four forms — widening (automatic, safe), narrowing (explicit, risky), upcasting (the engine of polymorphism), and downcasting (carefully controlled access to subclass features) — gives you precise control over how values and objects flow through your programs.

Professional Java code treats casting with discipline: widen freely where the type system allows, narrow consciously with range awareness, upcast to design flexible polymorphic APIs, and downcast sparingly with instanceof — preferably using pattern matching instanceof (Java 16+) to eliminate ClassCastException risk in one elegant expression. Frequent downcasting in business logic is a signal to revisit the design — polymorphism usually offers a cleaner alternative.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions — Java Type Casting

items.q: What is type casting in Java?
items.a: Type casting is converting a value from one data type to another. Two categories: primitive casting (between 8 primitive types) and object casting (between types in an inheritance hierarchy). Two directions: widening (smaller to larger, implicit, safe) and narrowing (larger to smaller, explicit, possible data loss). Object directions: upcasting (subclass to superclass, implicit, safe) and downcasting (superclass to subclass, explicit, may throw ClassCastException).

items.q: What is the difference between widening and narrowing casting in Java?
items.a: Widening: smaller → larger type, automatic (no cast operator), no data loss, safe. Order: byte→short→int→long→float→double. Example: int i=5; double d=i; // d=5.0. Narrowing: larger → smaller type, manual (cast operator required), possible data loss (truncation/overflow), risky. Example: double d=9.99; int i=(int)d; // i=9, decimal lost.

items.q: What is upcasting and downcasting in Java?
items.a: Upcasting: subclass reference → superclass reference. Implicit. Always safe. Enables polymorphism. Example: Animal a = new Dog(); — automatic. After upcasting, only superclass members accessible (but overridden methods still call subclass version at runtime). Downcasting: superclass reference → subclass reference. Explicit with (SubclassType). May throw ClassCastException. Always use instanceof first. Modern: if (a instanceof Dog d) { d.fetch(); } — pattern matching (Java 16+).

items.q: What is ClassCastException in Java?
items.a: ClassCastException is a RuntimeException thrown when downcasting an object to an incompatible type. Example: Animal a = new Cat(); Dog d = (Dog) a; — throws ClassCastException at runtime (Cat is not a Dog). Compiler allows the syntax (they share a hierarchy); JVM detects the mismatch at runtime. Prevention: always use instanceof before downcasting. Null can always be cast to any reference type without ClassCastException.

items.q: What is the instanceof operator and pattern matching in Java?
items.a: instanceof checks at runtime if an object is an instance of a specific type (returns true/false; false for null). Classic use: if (a instanceof Dog) { Dog d = (Dog) a; d.fetch(); }. Pattern matching (Java 16+): if (a instanceof Dog d) { d.fetch(); } — combines check and cast in one expression. The variable d is automatically bound within the if-block. Java 21 extends to switch patterns: switch(a) { case Dog d -> d.fetch(); case Cat c -> c.purr(); }.
